Working from home should be a right, not a reward. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Australian state of Victoria was due to enforce a legal right to work from home starting September 2026. But just weeks away from its implementation, the new premier, Ben Carroll, has announced a year’s delay in response to fierce business opposition.
Thousands of miles away, in Portugal, parents of young children already have a legal right to work from home without needing their employers’ approval.
All of these developments raise the question: Should workers be given a legal right to work from home?
There is an argument that firms should have full discretion over their employees’ working arrangements, including whether they can work remotely.
However, by giving bosses complete control over such decisions, we are in danger of affirming the importance of profitability over well-being and ignoring the needs of working parents.
Workers’ well-being
One justification for taking remote work policy out of bosses’ hands is to boost workers’ well-being. There are plenty of reasons why you might want to work remotely.
Maybe you want to avoid a long, sweaty, and costly commute. Maybe you like to go on a jog during your lunchbreak. Maybe you need to pick up your child from school.
When bosses have full control over their remote work policy, your preferences can be treated as irrelevant to that decision.
Sceptics might push back that if bosses were to bend to workers’ will, this would harm productivity. The pursuit of profit is arguably the best way to guarantee productivity growth. This expands the economic pie, from which we all benefit; a rising tide lifts all boats.
The question of whether remote work is bad for productivity is hotly contested. But let’s suppose that it is. Even so, productivity isn’t the only thing that we care about, surely.
Presumably, we also care about people’s well-being. And since many people’s well-being would be improved by having the option to work remotely, it seems odd to give this consideration no weight.
This is especially so, given that bosses can decide where their employees work based on fairly arbitrary reasons. For example, a recent study found that “narcissistic leaders” often demand their workers return to the office simply to boost their ego.
A cynic might nevertheless protest that workers can always leave: If your firm doesn’t let you work remotely, you can join another one that does.
But how easy is it to leave, really?
Moving jobs often requires changing location, retraining, and so on -- and landing a new job is no easy feat.
In the meantime, a right to work from home would protect workers from being subject to their bosses’ whims.
A further reason to enshrine a right to work from home is to promote gender equality.
When women have children, they often move to lower-paid part-time work or drop out of the labour force altogether. This is a major driver of the gender pay gap and can leave women dangerously dependent on their partners for financial support.
Working from home reduces the gender pay gap by enabling mothers in remote-compatible jobs to keep their careers alongside doing the school run. While this primarily helps women with office jobs, it’s still better than nothing.
That said, social scientists have warned that having the option to work from home can harm women by creating a new glass ceiling: Mothers self-select into remote work, and remote workers get promoted less.
On this basis, the economist Nicholas Bloom has argued that employers should not give their employees any say over which days they work from home.
But this argument rests on a mistake. It is true that the option to work from home may result in a two track trajectory where women are disproportionately set back in their careers.
But the likely alternative, where there is no option to work from home, is even worse for these same women.
Another concern is that if women choose to work from home, they could end up doing more housework and childcare. But the solution is not to deny people the option to work remotely, but instead to change outdated gender norms.
Innovative policies are also available: In Portugal, under the work from home policy, parents of young children in remote-compatible jobs must take it in turns to work remotely, so it isn’t always the mother who stays home.
Bosses are clawing workers back with return-to-office mandates. Many don’t care about promoting workers’ well-being and gender equality -- unless, of course, it impacts their bottom line.
But society should care. And these ideals are better served by at least partially taking the choice out of employers’ hands.
We stand at a fork in the road. Should we continue to let firms roll back the option to work from home, or should governments step in?
One thing’s for sure: The case for letting bosses decide isn’t as straightforward as it may initially seem.
Rebecca L Clark is a Postdoctoral Fellow in Philosophy, London School of Economics and Political Science. This article first appeared in The Conversation and is being republished under special arrangement.

The untold story of Bangladeshi tea. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Tea is a familiar drink, and yet it is far more than a luxury. Behind its aroma and its bitterness lies the maturity of a culture, born of climate, soil, people, trade, and faith.
I have visited tea plantations in India, Japan, and Bangladesh. Tea is a living thing rooted in the land, and it also reflects a nation's philosophy. Every country expresses its own philosophy through tea. Bangladeshi tea, for all its quality, has yet to appear on the world's tea map, and it is a shame that it remains so little known.
As the Cha Jing, the Classic of Tea written in the eighth century, tells us, tea was established as a philosophical system more than 1,200 years ago.
Tea is a ritual that joins heaven, earth, and people, and a culture in its own right. Across China's vast territory a rich variety of teas thrives: Oolong in Fujian, Pu'er in Yunnan, Longjing in Zhejiang. In recent years teahouses, tea art, and even tea utensils have been exported strategically as tourism resources, proof of how mature the country has become as a cultural industry.
The way China now extends the qualifications of its tea masters and tea tasters overseas holds real lessons for other countries.
Indian tea spread in the nineteenth century under the British East India Company as a pillar of colonial management, and it grew from the Assam variety, a plant native to the region itself. Assam, Darjeeling, Nilgiri. The place names themselves are now brands.
Darjeeling in particular has been called the champagne of tea, its muscatel aroma bound up with aristocratic culture.
Yet the shadows of colonialism remain: Low wages, land disparity, the strain on the environment. Fair trade and organic practices have made progress in recent years, but it will take time before tea truly becomes a source of national pride.
India is both a mirror and a warning for Bangladesh. From a production center to a cultural center. That transition will decide its future.
Tea seeds reached Japan with Zen monks in the late twelfth century, and in the sixteenth century Sen no Rikyu raised tea to an aesthetic, governed by the principles of harmony, respect, purity, and tranquility.
Tea reflects the state of the mind more than the taste on the tongue, and the freedom of a once in a lifetime encounter lives inside the formality of the tea ceremony.
As an industry, Shizuoka, Uji, Sayama, Yame, and other regions have built local brands, many of them now protected by GI certification. Demand for matcha has spread across the world, so much so that it has become hard to buy even at home.
Outside matcha, though, the domestic market keeps shrinking in both consumption and production as its farmers age, and a cultural revival is underway through matcha sweets and tourist tea plantations.
The key to the future lies in seeing matcha once again as a drink that nurtures the soul.
The tea fields of Bangladesh. Standing among the hills of Sylhet, Juri, and Srimangal, one is left breathless by their potential.
The hills, wrapped in mist, run on into Assam, yet the aroma is more delicate, closer to a Darjeeling.
A floral fragrance, a lingering citrus finish. It would be a shame to let such a tea stay unknown.
In 2025 the country produced about 94.9 million kilograms of tea yet exported only 1.64 million, down from 2.45 million the year before. The leaf is there. What is missing is the story to tell.
This country has strengths of its own. A young and hardworking workforce, a generous climate, a range of teas from black to white, and the smiles of its people.
Bring these together and it could stand as the champagne of the East. What it needs is a story, and the context to carry it.
The tea plantations of Bangladesh, woven of light and people, embody a quiet poetry of labor.
The first step is place of origin, and the acquisition of GI, geographical indication. Names like Sylhet Tea or Juri Valley Tea create stories of their own. Bangladesh now has 64 GI registered products, and tea is not among them. Moulvibazar, the heart of tea country, has already registered its agarwood, so the district knows the procedure. And the dispute over the Tangail saree showed what happens when a name goes unregistered.
Alongside registration, a tasting system staffed by experts would make quality visible. Tea should take root as a domestic culture before it is exported, in city cafes and tourist tea salons. And its stories can travel through photographs, film, and essays, until tea becomes a culture people talk about.
There is much to learn from Japanese tea making, from China's way of spreading its culture, from India's branding, on the way to a tea art in a Bangladeshi style. Bangladesh already has one curiosity all its own: Seven layer tea, seven strata standing in a single glass, poured by the different densities of milk and syrup. But this is not enough. We must make people see the history of tea in Sylhet and Bangladesh that stands behind it.
Towards a fragrant future
Tea is an art of earth, people, and wind. Bangladeshi tea is a sleeping poem the world has yet to read.
The afternoon light on the hills of Sylhet, the smiles of people at their work. Those moments were proof that the tea was alive.
What the world wants now are things that nourish the soul. Bangladeshi tea comes closest to embodying that.
The question now is whether someone will step forward to tell the story.
I believe that one day the steam rising from the hills of Sylhet will warm teacups all over the world.
Izumi Osaragi is an IFJ-accredited Japanese photojournalist and visual artist whose award-winning works merge poetic composition with documentary insight to explore the boundaries between society and culture.

item.title: Funding is not all what you need to start a business. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In discussions about entrepreneurship, success is often associated with large investments. Stories of global business icons dominate headlines, creating the impression that entrepreneurship is reserved for a fortunate few with extraordinary resources.
Yet the reality is often very different. Many entrepreneurs are proving that strategic working can outweigh financial limitations.
In Bangladesh, where youth unemployment remains a concern and economic transformation is accelerating, understanding the practical foundations of entrepreneurship has become increasingly important.
The startup story of Apple Computer is an inspiring one, whilst the journey demonstrates that money alone does not create success.
When Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs founded Apple in 1976, they did not begin with enormous wealth or corporate backing. They started in a garage with limited resources.
One founder sold his old car, and another one had almost nothing to sell; he sold his calculator. They started their venture with this scant amount of money. Their success did not come from having money; it came from recognizing an opportunity and having the courage to pursue it.
Today, Apple is one of the world's most valuable companies, proving that great ideas and persistence can outweigh financial limitations.
There are also several examples in Bangladesh where entrepreneurs have initiated businesses without funds or with extremely limited resources.
For example, a person used to collect empty condensed milk cans from dustbins in Rangpur around 20 years ago. He sold those to the factories of “jarda” to make customized containers. He gradually employed some poor children to collect the tins to expand his earnings.
After a certain period, when he had accumulated capital, he started producing cans for those factories. Then he developed his own factory and became a millionaire within a few years.
The story once appeared in a renowned newspaper with the title – “Kouta theke Kotipoti.” The person became a wealthy businessman literally without any financial investment at the initial stage.
Whereas many people do not consider initiating ventures due to a lack of funds, these examples demonstrate that start-up capital is not necessarily an essential element for entrepreneurship.
Examining the experiences of many entrepreneurs, scholars have concluded that the quality or ability of entrepreneurs is the most important determining factor for business prospects.
The opportunity lying in the market is the second crucial aspect. An entrepreneur with an excellent management team can turn the opportunity in favor of their firms.
The third critical element is resources, whereas people are mostly concerned about funding for starting their businesses.
There is no denying that it might not be viable for all to start a business without any start-up capital, as the examples illustrate.
In that case, the question is how they can use their limited resources properly to initiate a venture. Certain key strategies can be considered in this regard.
One fundamental issue is that entrepreneurs should invest primarily in the major resources for starting their businesses, given their funding constraints. In doing so, they need to find out the key resources for their business.
For example, if someone is starting a software business, the essential resource is software engineers. The quality of the engineers cannot be compromised for this venture.
Hence, the required amount of money for hiring and maintaining them should be the priority for expenditure. The cost of office decoration and other expenses, which are not related to core activities, might not be considered seriously at the initial stage.
Another important issue is that entrepreneurs do not need to have all in-house production for initiating their ventures. They might outsource some of the things.
They can also manage equipment, tools, or many other things through renting or leasing. As explained earlier, Apple Computer emerged in a garage; not in a highly equipped, polished office or laboratory.
Starting with all things together requires significant investment, whilst this kind of estimation discourages entrepreneurs’ prospects.
Technology has emerged as another powerful equalizer in the entrepreneurial landscape. The digital revolution has transformed how businesses are created and managed. Today, a smartphone and an internet connection can provide access to customers, suppliers, marketing channels, and financial services.
Moreover, social media platforms, e-commerce marketplaces, digital payment systems, and freelance networks have significantly reduced the barriers to entry for new businesses.
Entrepreneurs no longer need expensive physical infrastructure to reach consumers. A small home-based enterprise can market products nationally, and in some cases internationally, through digital platforms.
In short, the need for physical platforms, movement for communication, and efforts for information gathering have been changed; consequently, traditional areas of expenditure have been reduced.
A common misconception is that entrepreneurs must wait for the perfect conditions before starting a business. In the view of many people, perfect conditions can be achieved with a large amount of money.
Many postpone their dreams while searching for funding. However, experience shows that successful ventures rarely begin under ideal circumstances.
The mindset of proper utilization of limited resources encourages creativity and resilience. Constraints often force entrepreneurs to think differently and find innovative solutions that larger organizations may overlook.
In Bangladesh, where access to capital can be challenging for many aspiring entrepreneurs, resourcefulness is particularly valuable. Small beginnings should not be viewed as weaknesses.
Instead, they can serve as testing grounds where ideas are refined, customer needs are better understood, and business models are strengthened before significant investments are made.
Dr Jasmine Jaim is a Professor at Institute of Business Administration, Jahangirnagar University, Bangladesh and an Associate Editor of the international journal: Gender, Work and Organization. Email: jaim.jas@gmail.com
